label: Mains electricity
summary: The 100–240 V AC in building wiring, sockets, generators and inverters. A few tens of milliamps across the chest can stop the heart. After a collapse the grid may be dead, but generators, solar systems and inverters can still make building wiring live, sometimes without warning.
signs: Plugs, sockets, switches, breaker panels and fuse boxes
Appliance cords, and cables entering a building
A generator, inverter or solar system anywhere nearby
Lights, fans or chargers working: something is supplying power
Warm or scorched sockets, buzzing, or a smell of hot plastic
do: Unplug a device before opening it
Switch off at the main breaker or disconnect, then test with a meter before touching
Prove your meter on a known live source before and after testing
Tape or lock the switch off and leave a note so nobody turns it back on
Keep one hand away from the work
Work on a dry floor, with dry hands
dont: Don't trust wire colours, switches, or 'the power has been off for weeks'
Don't work on wet floors or with wet hands
Don't replace a fuse with wire or a bigger fuse
Don't connect a generator to a building through a socket: it can kill whoever works on the wiring
Don't open a live breaker panel
Don't touch someone who is being shocked
Don't step into standing water in a building that might have power from any source
ppe: No rings, watches or metal bracelets
Don’t count on boots: EH-rated soles are back-up only, to 600 V, dry and not worn through; ordinary rubber soles have no rating
firstAid: Switch off the power, or push the person free with dry wood or plastic, before touching them
If they aren't breathing normally, start CPR and keep going, and use a defibrillator (AED) as soon as one can be found
Anyone who took a shock across the chest, passed out or has burns needs medical care: heart rhythm problems can start hours later
Electrical burns go deeper than they look; cool with clean water and cover loosely
